interface.name: inox_shell_v1

description.summary: shell surfaces for Inox's own desktop components

interface.description:
Private, unstable Inox protocol for the surfaces that *are* the desktop: the panel, its menu bar, the dock, and the menus they open.
Why this protocol exists at all. `zwlr-layer-shell-unstable-v1` and `xdg-shell` can place a surface at the edge of an output and can hang an `xdg_popup` off it, and for a third-party panel that is enough. They stop being enough the moment the shell wants to behave like one continuous object instead of a set of unrelated rectangles:
- A layer surface is placed but never *animated*. A panel and the menu it opens are two surfaces; when one becomes the other, or when a menu grows out of the button that opened it, only the compositor can draw the frames in between, because only it knows when a surface is actually shown, at what scale, over which backdrop. Layer-shell has no way to ask for that, and a client cannot animate across its own surface boundary — everything it draws is clipped to the rectangle it was configured to. - An `xdg_popup` exists inside `xdg-shell`'s model of a menu: it is grabbed with a serial that came from a real input event, its positioner is fixed at creation, and it is only legal after the parent mapped. A shell menu opened from the keyboard, re-laid-out when the work area changes, or nested three levels deep does not fit that model, and a panel that is deliberately not keyboard-interactive (D01: ordinary presentation must not steal focus) cannot hand its popup a keyboard at all. - The work area a panel has to lay itself out against is not something a layer surface is ever told. It changes when another surface reserves space, when the output is resized, when the panel is reloaded, and the shell has to guess or poll. - A shell surface whose backdrop is frosted (`inox-glass-v1`) is frost eligible only because it has a *layer* role. Popups and any future shell surface would each need an exception, and a menu that opens over a frosted panel double-frosts the same pixels.
So this protocol owns the shell role end to end: placement, the shell keyboard model, popups with compositor-driven dismissal, the work-area event, and motion hints the compositor draws. It is deliberately narrow: it only describes surfaces with a desktop layer, and it grants no readback, no capture and no input injection.
Relationship to the standard protocols. `zwlr-layer-shell-unstable-v1` stays advertised for third-party panels and bars; Inox's own components use this protocol instead, and support for layer-shell is not a fallback for them. Session locking does *not* move here: `ext-session- lock-v1` carries security semantics (no content may be visible before the locked frame is presented on every output) that must not be re-implemented by an unstable private protocol. Lock surfaces stay `ext_session_lock_v1` surfaces; the lock client's *rendering* becomes a native Qt client like the panel's, without a new role.
Two objects, two kinds of "menu". A `menu`-role *surface* is the shell's own placed surface that belongs to another shell surface — a launcher anchored to the panel button that opened it, or a popover that needs its own work area and its own animation. It is placed like any shell surface and is not grabbed. A `inox_shell_popup_v1` is the transient kind: the compositor dismisses it on a click outside, on Escape, or when its parent hides. The two exist separately because their lifetimes differ — a launcher that closed whenever the user clicked elsewhere would not be a launcher.
Lifetime and failure. A `inox_shell_surface_v1` describes a role for one `wl_surface`; the surface belongs to the compositor's shell layer stack until it is destroyed, the client disconnects, or the compositor closes it. A compositor that cannot honour a request (no room for the exclusive zone, an effect it does not implement, a popup whose parent is gone) reports it through `capabilities`, `configure` or `dismissed` — never by silently drawing something else, because the shell decides its fallback from those answers.
This protocol is an Inox extension and is not part of the upstream wayland-protocols. It is unstable until Inox 1.0: interfaces may change in a backwards-incompatible way, and consumers must negotiate through the `capabilities` event instead of assuming a fixed revision.
Warning! The protocol described in this file is currently in the testing phase. Backward compatible changes may be added together with the corresponding interface version bump. Backward incompatible changes can be done by creating a new version of this protocol.

enum.name: capability

description.summary: optional parts of this protocol a compositor implements

enum.description: Reported by the `capabilities` event. A compound compositor sets every bit it implements; a client must check the bits it depends on and fall back to an instant, unanimated presentation for anything missing. Bits this client does not know are ignored, so the field can grow without a version bump.

entry.name: transitions
entry.summary: enter/exit transitions are drawn by the compositor

entry.name: popup_keyboard
entry.summary: a popup can be granted the keyboard independently of its parent

entry.name: workarea
entry.summary: the workarea event is sent and kept up to date

entry.name: nested_popups
entry.summary: a popup may be the parent of another popup (submenus)

enum.name: surface_role

description.summary: what the shell surface is, semantically

enum.description: A role is a semantic label, not a position: where the surface goes is described by `set_placement`. The compositor uses the role for policy that must not be guessable from geometry — which surfaces a lock hides, which ones the shell's own keyboard model reaches, and which ones a future shell animation may move as one group.

entry.name: panel
entry.summary: a standing bar: taskbar, menu bar, status area

entry.name: dock
entry.summary: an application dock, usually floating above the work area

entry.name: overlay
entry.summary: a full-output shell surface: launcher, switcher, a morph host

entry.name: menu
entry.summary: a shell-owned surface that belongs to another shell surface

request.name: destroy

description.summary: destroy the shell object

request.description: Destroy the factory. Shell surfaces it created stay valid: they belong to the surfaces they were created for, not to this object.

request.name: get_surface

description.summary: assign the shell role to a surface

request.description:
Assign a shell role to `surface` and return the object that describes it. The surface must not have a role yet and must not have been committed with a buffer: the compositor decides the size, and a client that already drew at its own size has guessed wrong.
A shell surface is *placed* by its client and *sized* by the compositor: the client sends `set_placement` and commits without a buffer, the compositor answers `configure`, and from then on the surface is mapped and drawn at the configured size. A client that detaches its buffer unmaps the surface and must go through `configure` again, exactly as a layer surface does.

arg.name: surface
arg.summary: the surface that becomes a shell surface

event.name: capabilities

description.summary: what this compositor implements of this protocol

event.description:
Sent once when the object is created, before any request on it is answered. `capabilities` is a bitfield of `capability`; `max_transition_duration` is the longest enter/exit transition the compositor will animate, in milliseconds, and is 0 when it animates none.
A client must not ask for an effect it was not offered: requesting a slide where the compositor only fades would make the shell and the compositor disagree about what the user is looking at, and the shell is the half that has to keep its own animations consistent with it.

arg.name: capabilities
arg.summary: implemented optional parts of this protocol

arg.name: max_transition_duration
arg.summary: longest animated transition, milliseconds; 0 if none

interface.name: inox_shell_surface_v1

description.summary: one shell surface: placement, keyboard model and motion

interface.description:
One shell surface. It is created by `inox_shell_v1.get_surface` and lives as long as its `wl_surface`.
State is committed, not applied on arrival: `set_placement`, `set_keyboard` and `set_transition` describe the surface's desired state and take effect on the next `wl_surface.commit`. This is the same rule layer-shell uses, and it is what makes a reload that changes four values at once look like one change rather than four.
Placement is sent as one request rather than as six setters. A shell surface is placed as a unit — anchor and margin and exclusive zone only mean something together — and splitting them lets a compositor observe half of a placement, reserve the wrong strip, and then correct itself on the next commit. One request, one consistent state.

enum.name: layer

description.summary: the shell layer this surface is drawn in

enum.description: Layers are ordered back to front. Shell surfaces of different roles may share a layer; within a layer the compositor keeps its own stacking order, which the client must not depend on.

entry.name: background
entry.summary: wallpaper-like content

entry.name: bottom
entry.summary: below ordinary windows

entry.name: top
entry.summary: above ordinary windows

entry.name: overlay
entry.summary: above everything, including other shell surfaces

enum.name: anchor

description.summary: which edges of the work area the surface is attached to

enum.description: Anchor bits are combined. Anchoring to one edge pins that edge and leaves the other axis to the surface's own size; anchoring to opposite edges stretches the surface between them unless a size was requested; anchoring to nothing centres the surface.

entry.name: top
entry.summary: the top edge

entry.name: bottom
entry.summary: the bottom edge

entry.name: left
entry.summary: the left edge

entry.name: right
entry.summary: the right edge

enum.name: keyboard_mode

description.summary: how this surface gets the keyboard

enum.description:
`none` is the default and the right choice for a panel that only presents: D01 requires ordinary presentation not to steal focus, so a panel must be able to exist without ever being focused. A popup that needs keys asks for them itself through `inox_shell_popup_v1.set_keyboard`, which is what makes a keyboard- navigated menu possible out of a panel that never holds the keyboard.
`on_demand` gives the surface ordinary focus semantics: the compositor may focus it when the user clicks it or navigates to it, and may take the focus away again. `exclusive` asks for the keyboard whenever the surface is mapped and on top; a compositor may still refuse, and it must report what it did through `keyboard_state`.

entry.name: none
entry.summary: never focused; pointer only

entry.name: on_demand
entry.summary: ordinary focus semantics

entry.name: exclusive
entry.summary: wants the keyboard whenever mapped on top

enum.name: effect

description.summary: an enter or exit transition

enum.description:
Effects are drawn by the compositor over the surface's own frames: the client renders its final state once, and the compositor fades, slides or scales it into place. A client that animates the same movement itself would fight the compositor for the same pixels, which is why requesting an effect and animating it client-side are alternatives, not layers.
`none` means "appear and disappear instantly" and is always available. A compositor reports which of the others it implements through `inox_shell_v1.capabilities`.

entry.name: none
entry.summary: no transition

entry.name: fade
entry.summary: cross-fade against the backdrop

entry.name: slide
entry.summary: move in from, and out towards, the origin edge

entry.name: scale
entry.summary: grow from, and shrink towards, the origin point

enum.name: curve

description.summary: the timing curve of a transition

enum.description: Named curves rather than parameters: the shell must not have to know the compositor's spring stiffness to get the same feel as the rest of the desktop, and a compositor that implements its own motion language maps these names onto it.

entry.name: linear
entry.summary: constant speed

entry.name: ease_out
entry.summary: fast start, settled end

entry.name: spring
entry.summary: slight overshoot, settled end

request.name: set_placement

description.summary: place the surface in the work area

request.description:
Describe where the surface goes. `layer` is the shell layer, `anchor` the edges it is attached to, `exclusive_zone` the strip the compositor must keep clear for it, `margin_*` the distances from those edges, and `width`/`height` the surface's requested size in its own logical coordinates, where 0 means "the compositor decides".
`exclusive_zone` follows layer-shell's meaning because users' muscle memory does: a positive value is the thickness to reserve on the anchored edge, 0 means "I want to be moved out of other surfaces' reserved strips but reserve nothing myself", and -1 means "do not move me, let me extend to the edge I am anchored to". A positive value on a surface that is not anchored to exactly one edge (or one edge plus its two perpendiculars) reserves nothing, because there is no strip that value could describe.
The compositor clamps the result to the output: a margin that pushes the surface off-screen is reduced, never honoured. The size in `configure` is authoritative — a client that asked for 1000x28 and is configured 800x28 must lay itself out for 800.

arg.name: exclusive_zone
arg.summary: strip to reserve, 0 for none, -1 to extend to the edge

arg.name: width
arg.summary: requested width, 0 to let the compositor decide

arg.name: height
arg.summary: requested height, 0 to let the compositor decide

request.name: set_keyboard

description.summary: how this surface wants the keyboard

request.description: Set the keyboard mode. The compositor answers with `keyboard_state` whenever it changes, and a popup's own request overrides what it would otherwise inherit — a panel that never takes focus can still own a menu that does.

request.name: set_transition

description.summary: ask the compositor to animate this surface in and out

request.description:
Ask for enter and exit transitions. The compositor animates the surface's own frames: it does not ask the client for intermediate states, so the client must render the final state and leave the motion to the compositor.
`duration` is in milliseconds and is clamped to the maximum reported by `inox_shell_v1.capabilities`; a duration of 0 disables the transition, which is also what a client that was not offered the requested effect must fall back to. `origin` is an anchor bitfield naming the point the slide or scale grows from — an empty mask means "the centre". `origin` has no meaning for `fade` and is ignored there.
Transitions are a hint, not a promise about pixels: a compositor that is shutting down, running without a renderer, or honouring the user's reduced-motion preference may drop them entirely. The shell must look right when every transition is instantaneous, which is why the protocol has no "transition finished" event for a client to wait on.

arg.name: origin
arg.summary: anchor point the transition grows from; empty means centre

request.name: get_popup

description.summary: create a popup belonging to this surface

request.description:
Create a popup whose parent is this surface. The popup is a normal `wl_surface` that gains the popup role; it is positioned relative to this surface, drawn above it, and dismissed with it.
Unlike `xdg_popup`, no input serial is involved: a shell menu is frequently opened from the keyboard, from a timer, or from a protocol event, and there is no serial to grab with. The popup's grab is a *policy* the compositor applies — see `set_dismissable` — not a transaction the client has to authorise.

arg.name: surface
arg.summary: the surface that becomes the popup

request.name: destroy

description.summary: destroy the shell surface object

request.description: Destroy the object. The `wl_surface` loses its shell role and is unmapped; the buffer is not touched. Popups of this surface are dismissed first, so a client does not have to tear down a menu tree by hand.

event.name: configure

description.summary: the size the surface should have

event.description:
Sent after every commit that changed placement, and whenever the compositor's own constraints changed (a work-area change, an output resize, a scale change). The client must ack the serial before the commit that answers it, exactly as a layer surface does.
`width` and `height` are in the surface's logical coordinates and are the size the surface will be given; they are not a maximum. A client that draws at another size is showing the wrong thing, not a smaller version of the right thing.

event.name: workarea

description.summary: the area this surface's output leaves to clients

event.description:
The rectangle this surface may be laid out against, in the output's logical coordinates: the output minus every exclusive zone on it. It is sent once when the surface is created, and again whenever it changes — another shell surface reserving space, a window going fullscreen, an output being resized, the panel itself being reloaded with a different thickness.
This is the event layer-shell does not have. A shell that has to place a menu, clamp a tooltip or size a launcher needs the same rectangle the compositor used, and re-deriving it from configuration drifts the moment anything else reserves space.

event.name: keyboard_state

description.summary: whether this surface currently has the keyboard

event.description: Sent whenever the answer changes: 1 when this surface is receiving key events, 0 when it is not. A shell uses it to draw focus rings and to decide whether Escape belongs to it or to the window underneath, and it must not assume that asking for `exclusive` was granted.

event.name: closed

description.summary: the compositor will not show this surface

event.description: The surface is going away: its output was removed, the compositor is shutting this shell surface down, or the role no longer applies. After this event the object is inert and the client should destroy it. Unlike a layer surface's `closed`, this is also how the compositor reports that it refused the role outright, so a client that receives it before its first `configure` must not retry in a loop.

interface.name: inox_shell_popup_v1

description.summary: a shell popup: a menu, a tooltip, a nested submenu

interface.description:
A popup of a shell surface. It is drawn directly above its parent, positioned by its client, dismissed by the compositor, and it may itself be the parent of another popup — which is what makes submenus a nesting of the same object instead of a special case.
What a popup does *not* do is decide its own fate. It does not grab the pointer or the keyboard by asking for them at a moment of its choosing; it declares whether it is dismissable and whether it needs keys, and the compositor applies its policy: a click outside dismisses it, Escape dismisses it, its parent unmapping dismisses it. The client learns that it happened through `dismissed`, which is also the only signal it should use to animate its own exit — the compositor may have already started one.
Sizing. A popup is sized the way a shell surface is: the client asks for a size in `set_size`, the compositor answers `configure`, and the configured size is authoritative. A popup that is wider than the remaining work area is clamped by the compositor, and the client must lay out for the clamped width rather than assume its request.

request.name: set_position

description.summary: position the popup relative to its parent

request.description:
Place the popup's `popup_anchor` edge or corner at the parent's `parent_anchor` edge or corner, offset by `x` and `y` in the popup's logical coordinates. Two anchors rather than one is what makes a menu that flips — a submenu that would leave the work area opens to the left of its parent instead of the right — expressible without the client guessing where the compositor put the parent.
The compositor clamps the result to the work area and may flip the offset if that is the only way to fit. It never moves the popup into a position the client did not name without saying so: the popup's `configure` reports the size, and a client that must know the position reads it back from its own item geometry, not from the wire.

arg.name: popup_anchor
arg.summary: the popup's edge or corner placed on it

request.name: set_size

description.summary: request a size for the popup

request.description: Request the popup's size in its own logical coordinates; 0 lets the compositor decide that axis. The configured size is authoritative and may be smaller — a menu wider than the screen is clamped, not scaled.

arg.name: width
arg.summary: requested width, 0 to let the compositor decide

arg.name: height
arg.summary: requested height, 0 to let the compositor decide

request.name: set_keyboard

description.summary: whether the popup needs the keyboard

request.description: Ask for the keyboard while the popup is open. This is deliberately separate from the parent's keyboard mode: a panel that never takes focus (D01) still owns menus that must be navigated with Tab and Escape, and a compositor that grants keys to the popup must take them back when it dismisses the popup. The answer arrives as `keyboard_state` on this object, and a compositor that does not implement popup keyboards reports 0 forever rather than silently stealing focus from a window.

arg.name: needed
arg.summary: 1 to ask for the keyboard, 0 to release it

request.name: set_dismissable

description.summary: whether the compositor may dismiss this popup

request.description:
Declare whether a click outside this popup, an Escape key, or the parent going away should dismiss it. A menu sets 1; a passive tooltip sets 0 and closes itself.
A dismissable popup implies a pointer grab that only the compositor can take: it must see the click that lands outside the popup even though that click belongs to another client's surface, and it must consume it so the window underneath does not also act on it. This is why dismissal is a compositor policy in this protocol instead of the client-owned grab xdg-shell describes.

arg.name: dismissable
arg.summary: 1 if the compositor may dismiss it

request.name: dismiss

description.summary: close the popup

request.description: Ask the compositor to close this popup and everything nested in it. The compositor runs the popup's exit transition and then discards the surface; the client must not destroy the `wl_surface` itself while the exit is running, and must wait for the object's destruction instead of assuming the request was immediate.

request.name: set_transition

description.summary: animate this popup in and out

request.description: Same semantics as `inox_shell_surface_v1.set_transition`, with one difference: the default origin is the anchor this popup was positioned with, so a menu grows out of the item that opened it without the client having to repeat the anchor here.

request.name: get_popup

description.summary: create a nested popup (a submenu) of this popup

request.description: Create a popup whose parent is this popup. Nesting is the same object again: a submenu is positioned relative to the item that opened it, drawn above its parent, dismissed with it, and counted in the same dismissal stack the compositor unwinds.

arg.name: surface
arg.summary: the surface that becomes the nested popup

request.name: destroy

description.summary: destroy the popup object

request.description: Destroy the object and unmap its surface. Nested popups are dismissed first.

event.name: configure

description.summary: the size the popup should have

event.description: Sent after the popup's placement or size request was committed, and whenever the work area changed such that the clamp changed. The client must ack the serial before the commit that answers it.

event.name: dismissed

description.summary: the compositor dismissed this popup

event.description: The compositor is closing this popup. The surface will be unmapped after its exit transition; the client should drop whatever state it was showing and must not try to re-open the same popup as part of handling this event, because that is how a menu that refuses to close is written.

event.name: keyboard_state

description.summary: whether this popup currently has the keyboard

event.description: Sent whenever the answer changes: 1 while key events reach the popup, 0 when they do not. A menu uses it to decide whether it owns Escape and the arrow keys, or whether those belong to the window underneath.
